November 11, 2026

 

Verify by Doing: Co-Evolving Agent Execution and Evaluation without
External Feedback

Yitong Lin^(1,2 \*)  Jianda Chen^(1 \*)  Yihao Hu¹  Pan Wang¹  Hang Wang¹  Zhihao Wen¹  Xiaoxue Ren²  Wei Wu¹

¹Ant International  ²Zhejiang University

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 1 Introduction

Agent self-improvement depends on feedback that identifies successful
attempts and guides updates to the procedures that produce them. At test
time, agents can update their workflows or harnesses while keeping model
weights fixed ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1); [Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)), or use additional inference to generate and check
more candidates ([Snell et al., 2025](#bib.bib25); [Brown et al.,
2024](#bib.bib3)). Both strategies depend on reliable feedback about
whether the task has been completed. Beyond standardized benchmarks,
reference answers and task completion signals may be unavailable,
leaving the task request and observations from environment interaction
as the main basis for verification.

This setting creates two coupled challenges: inferring task success from
incomplete observations, and improving the agent when the resulting
feedback may itself be incomplete. The budget example in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction") illustrates why both
matter: finding expected labels does not establish task completion,
while generating more outputs under the same checks can preserve the
same blind spots. This motivates active verification and adaptation of
the verification procedure.

Existing methods address parts of these challenges. Tool-based critique
can acquire additional observations ([Gou et al., 2024](#bib.bib9)), and
retrospective diagnosis and preference history can guide updates to
actor procedures ([Pan et al., 2026](#bib.bib18); [Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14); [Nie et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)), but they do not
update the verification procedure itself.

![Refer to caption](2611.15276v1/teaser_budget.png)

Figure 1: Active verification of a budget workbook. The task requires
correct payer assignments, consistent expense totals, and after-tax
revenue. Initial checks inspect labels and headers; an updated Evaluator
skill retrieves expense and revenue cells while the workbook remains
selected. Offline recomputation checks expense totals and after-tax
revenue from the retrieved cells.

Incomplete verification can leave blind spots unresolved and misguide
later adaptation ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib26)). Red Queen Gödel
Machine jointly evolves agents and evaluators, using held-out ground
truth to guide Evaluator replacement ([Iacob et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)).
We study within-task adaptation where execution and verification evolve
without external feedback from benchmark scores or labeled references.

We introduce Verify by Doing (VbD), which couples task execution with
active verification. The Actor executes the task through an editable
harness of instructions, skills, and working checks, while the Evaluator
uses its own harness to inspect artifacts and environment state,
recording satisfied, violated, and unresolved requirements. These
findings ground preferences between task results and guide updates to
both harnesses. Updating the verification procedure changes how this
internal signal is produced, while requirements remain fixed.

After initialization, VbD tests retained and proposed Actor harnesses in
the task environment (Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction")).
Each trial produces a candidate comprising an execution record,
resulting state, and response or deliverable. Proposed Evaluators are
reviewed against the retained version on the same candidates, comparing
the evidential support and applicable criteria in their reports. The
retained Evaluator’s findings guide output selection, while Actor
adoption separately requires support for the proposed harness’s own
fresh output. An Editor uses the findings, comparison decisions, and
task history to propose further updates to either or both harnesses.

VbD makes three contributions:

- •
  Active verification: verify by doing. Tool-based inspections gather
  evidence of task completion from artifacts and environment state.
- •
  Evidence-driven harness co-evolution. Shared findings guide Actor and
  Evaluator harness updates within a single task.
- •
  Comparative review and separate retention. Trials and report
  comparisons support separate decisions for Evaluator adoption,
  candidate selection, and Actor retention.

Across AutomationBench, $`\tau^{3}`$ Banking, and selected GDPval
tasks ([Patwardhan et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)), VbD achieves the highest
overall scores among the compared methods without external feedback on
two backbones. Ablations support the contributions of active
verification and Evaluator evolution, with positive mean gains on all
three task sets. Holding BoN candidates fixed, the retained Evaluator
improves pass rate and partial credit over the initial Evaluator,
demonstrating better selection from the same candidate outputs. Case
studies connect verification findings to execution improvements and
selection of earlier successful candidates, while revealing remaining
errors in evidence interpretation.

![Refer to caption](2611.15276v1/vbd_overall.png)

Figure 2: Verify by Doing overview. Verification findings provide

## 2 Related Work

#### Improving agent procedures.

Agent improvement methods differ in what they update and how feedback
guides those updates. DSPy optimizes modular language-model pipelines,
while AFlow searches code-represented workflows ([Khattab et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). Voyager
accumulates executable skills through environment feedback ([Wang
et al., 2023](#bib.bib27)). Self-Refine and Reflexion improve outputs or
later behavior ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib16); [Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib23)). GEPA evolves prompts, while DGM, HGM, and
Hyperagents edit agent programs or improvement procedures ([Agrawal
et al., 2026](#bib.bib1); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib35); [Wang
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib28); [Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib36)).
Self-Harness accepts edits using regression tests ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib34)); ModularRSI combines program checks, overfitting
review, and execution checks ([Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)). Several
methods adapt harnesses without labeled validation signals. RHO
diagnoses past rollouts and selects harnesses for future tasks using a
fixed self-preference ranking procedure ([Pan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18)). RHI revises a task-specific textual harness from
pairwise preference history under a fixed evaluation prompt ([Lee
et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)); TTHE edits executable harnesses from
unlabeled traces ([Nie et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)). In contrast, VbD uses
verification findings to update both Actor and Evaluator harnesses.

#### Obtaining evidence for judgment.

Judging task completion can require observations beyond the Actor’s
trace. ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions that gather external
information ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib32)). CRITIC uses tools to
critique outputs, Self-RAG learns retrieval and critique decisions, and
LATS combines environment feedback with search ([Gou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib9); [Asai et al., 2023](#bib.bib2); [Zhou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib40)). Agent-as-a-Judge inspects artifacts against
requirements, while VAGEN actively probes graphical interface
state ([Zhuge et al., 2025](#bib.bib42); [Cui et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)).
The Verification Horizon studies informative verification as generation
changes; AIChilles searches for workloads exposing regressions ([Wang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib26); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)). Studies of
intrinsic self-correction report failures without external
feedback ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)), while ProCo improves
correction through structured condition verification ([Wu et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib31)). VbD carries inspection findings into later rounds
as proposed changes to both execution and verification.

#### Co-evolving execution and evaluation.

Process supervision trains reward models with human feedback on
intermediate reasoning steps ([Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib15)).
Other training approaches couple generation with learned rewards or
feedback on judgments ([Yuan et al., 2024](#bib.bib33); [Wu et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib30)); related work studies rubric learning and
prover–verifier interaction ([Ding et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Kirchner
et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)). At the program level, RQGM co-evolves agents
and evaluators through controlled utility evolution: evaluation remains
fixed within each search stage and changes at qualified
boundaries ([Iacob et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). Its shared workspaces
also permit edits affecting both roles. Double Ratchet selects evolving
metrics with an anchored reference set ([Zhang et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib38)). VbD uses active verification to couple execution
and verification updates within a task, without external feedback.
Comparative review evaluates evolving feedback procedures before they
guide output selection and Actor retention decisions separately.

## 3 Problem Setting

We study agent improvement within a task $`x`$, given its request,
materials, and permitted tools. Each Actor candidate links an execution
record, resulting state, and response or deliverable to its generating
harness. Benchmark outcomes, official rubrics, and expert outputs are
reserved for offline scoring.

Actor harness $`H`$ and Evaluator harness $`\Phi`$ contain instructions,
working rubrics, and skills. Rubrics express checks against public
requirements: Actor rubrics guide execution and self-checks; Evaluator
rubrics guide assessment. Skills specify execution or verification
procedures. $`H`$ also includes persistent check plans, distinct from
temporary trial questions. Model weights, task requirements,
permissions, editor, selector, and reviewer instructions, eligibility,
and acceptance rules remain fixed.

The retained state includes an incumbent candidate $`z`$, candidate set
$`\mathcal{G}`$, and history $`\mathcal{D}`$. The incumbent need not
come from the current Actor. Harnesses and history reset between tasks;
the final output is frozen before scoring.

## 4 Verify by Doing

VbD addresses the two challenges in Section [1](#S1 "1 Introduction") by
making verification both active and adaptable. Inspection supplies
evidence for judging current outputs; the same findings guide changes to
how the Actor executes and how the Evaluator checks completion. Because
both procedures evolve, VbD reviews verification changes before
selection and evaluates Actor changes through fresh trials.

Initialization inspects two attempts from the initial Actor and selects
an incumbent without adopting updates. The editor prepares proposals if
another round remains. Subsequent rounds follow
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction"): Actor Trials, Agentic
Evaluation, Comparative Selection, and Harness Co-evolution. A tilde
denotes a proposal; a superscript $`+`$ denotes retained state.

### 4.1 Actor Trials

A verification finding identifies a potential improvement, but the
proposed harness must be tested through execution. Following harness
optimization ([Pan et al., 2026](#bib.bib18); [Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)), Step 1 runs the current Actor $`H`$ and proposed
Actor $`\widetilde{H}`$ to produce fresh candidates $`a`$ and $`b`$.
Both receive the same temporary checks; only the proposal uses
persistent edits. This exposes both Actors to the current verification
concerns while testing the proposed execution procedure. Temporary
checks expire after the round unless reconsidered. Without a proposal,
both attempts use $`H`$.

Each candidate preserves its execution record, resulting state, and
response or deliverable for subsequent verification. We append the
candidates to $`\mathcal{G}`$ and record their generating harnesses.
This link matters because an updated Evaluator may select an earlier
output: selecting that output provides no trial evidence for adopting
the proposed Actor. Fresh trials instead provide execution evidence for
the separate retention decision in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing").

### 4.2 Agentic Evaluation

To judge completion from incomplete observations, Step 2 gathers
evidence about the effects of execution. Each Evaluator independently
inspects a common pool $`\mathcal{B}`$, locating relevant state or
artifacts and executing checks for unresolved requirements. Workbook
cell reads, for example, expose relationships left untested by header
checks (Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction")). Findings take
the form

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{F}_{\Phi}(\mathcal{B})=\{(c_{i},q_{i},o_{i},f_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m},
``` |  | (1) |

where each of the $`m`$ findings records a candidate
$`c_{i}\in\mathcal{B}`$, proposition $`q_{i}`$, observations and sources
$`o_{i}`$, and scoped assessment $`f_{i}`$ with uncertainty. Payer
attribution requires linking a value to its source record.
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction") distinguishes Field,
Relation, Aggregate, and Task scopes.

A fixed selector $`\Pi`$ interprets these findings against the request:

|     |                                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       d=\Pi\bigl(x,\mathcal{B},\mathcal{F}_{\Phi}(\mathcal{B})\bigr).
       ```                                                              |     | (2) |

Record $`d`$ names a candidate and distinguishes supported preferences,
ties, unresolved judgments, and fallbacks. Its preference supplies the
internal signal; the findings guide execution and verification updates.
Updating $`\Phi`$ changes how evidence is acquired and assessed while
the task $`x`$ and selector $`\Pi`$ stay fixed.

### 4.3 Comparative Selection

Incomplete checks can favor outputs that miss requirements ([Skalse
et al., 2022](#bib.bib24); [Gao et al., 2023](#bib.bib8)). Adapting
verification can reveal missed requirements but also changes the basis
for judging Actor improvement. Step 3 therefore tests the proposed
Evaluator on common candidates, uses the retained procedure to select an
output, and requires support for the Actor’s fresh output before
adoption.

#### Evaluator adoption.

A fixed reviewer tests whether the proposed verification procedure
produces better-supported findings on the same candidates. It compares
evidential support, criterion applicability, and counterexamples in the
two reports. Both orders are reviewed to reduce sensitivity to position
bias ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib39)). Let $`V_{E}`$ indicate a
completed valid trial and $`v_{1},v_{2}`$ be votes mapped to Evaluator
identities:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Phi^{+}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{\Phi},&V_{E}\land v_{1}=v_{2}=\widetilde{\Phi},\\
\Phi,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (3) |

Without a tested proposal, $`V_{E}`$ is false and the current Evaluator
is retained.

#### Output selection.

The retained Evaluator supports selection from the eligible candidates
$`\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{G}`$, with further inspection as needed.
Qualification and selection may use different candidate sets
(Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1 "Comparison stages and candidate sets. ‣ B.1 Execution Schedule ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle d^{+}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Pi\bigl(x,\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F}_{\Phi^{+}}(\mathcal{C})\bigr),`$ |  | (4) |
|  | $`\displaystyle z^{+}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{out}(d^{+}).`$ |  |  |

Here $`\operatorname{out}`$ returns the named candidate, including a
fallback representative. Improved verification can select an earlier
successful output even when fresh attempts fail.

#### Actor retention.

Actor adoption requires support for the proposal’s own fresh candidate.
Let $`V_{A}`$ denote a valid trial of a changed Actor. Indicators
$`s_{1},s_{2}`$ record strict support in the initial comparison (or
candidate-set selection) and the subsequent incumbent comparison, each
requiring agreement in both presentation orders:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
H^{+}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{H},&V_{A}\land(z^{+}=b)\land s_{1}\land s_{2},\\
H,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (5) |

Condition $`z^{+}=b`$ requires selection of the proposal’s own output;
$`s_{1}\land s_{2}`$ excludes fallback choices. Selecting an earlier
output leaves the Actor unchanged. This rule holds across main
experiments and ablations
(Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Execution Schedule ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")).

### 4.4 Harness Co-evolution

To carry a verification finding into later attempts, Step 4 translates
it into a proposed change to execution, verification, or both. The fixed
editor $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edit}}`$ specifies an expected effect and
a corresponding check for the next trial. Retrieving a supposedly
unavailable contact sheet
(Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction")), for example, supplies
an Actor retrieval instruction and an Evaluator check for future
unavailability claims. The same observation can therefore provide both
execution guidance and a verification procedure.

After appending attempts, proposals, and decisions to history
$`\mathcal{D}^{+}`$, the editor prepares proposals if another round
remains:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\widetilde{H}_{\mathrm{next}},\widetilde{\Phi}_{\mathrm{next}})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{edit}}(x,H^{+},\Phi^{+},\mathcal{D}^{+}).
``` |  | (6) |

History preserves rejected trials and observation sources to inform
later proposals ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)); unchanged components
receive no update. Steps 1–3 evaluate these proposals, and their
findings guide subsequent edits. Inspection, adaptation, and review
connect Actor behavior, Evaluator checks, and the retention of changes.
After the final round, VbD returns the selected output
(Algorithm [1](#algorithm1 "In Appendix A Complete Evolution Procedure")).

## 5 Experiments

The results support VbD’s central premise: execution and its guiding
verification procedures benefit from evolving together. Overall gains,
fixed-candidate selection, and ablations support this design. Update
decisions distinguish output selection from Actor retention; cases and
behavioral changes connect verification findings to reusable execution
guidance and checks.

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

The three benchmarks require different evidence of task completion.
AutomationBench evaluates workflow execution through saved application
state on 600 tasks across six domains ([Shepard and Salimans,
2026](#bib.bib21)). $`\tau^{3}`$ Banking tests whether dialogue and
actions satisfy policy on 97 tasks ([Shi et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)).
GDPval assesses professional deliverables ([Patwardhan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)); we use 133 tasks supported by our text and document
tools.
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
gives the GDPval selection criteria.

Here, external feedback refers to benchmark scores or reference labels;
the internal signal is the preference inferred from verification
evidence
(Equation [2](#S4.E2 "In 4.2 Agentic Evaluation ‣ 4 Verify by Doing")).
We score final selected outputs by pass rate on AutomationBench and
Banking, and mean rubric quality on GDPval. Official checks, rubrics,
and expert outputs are reserved for offline scoring, except for the
reference with external feedback. GDPval’s rubric score differs from its
official expert pairwise win rate.

The main experiments use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 for all task roles with
frozen weights. Offline grading with language models uses GPT-5.6-sol
with xhigh reasoning effort. All iterative methods use two Actor
executions per round for three rounds, then freeze selected outputs for
offline scoring. VbD’s main experiments and ablations share comparative
Actor acceptance
(Equation [5](#S4.E5 "In Actor retention. ‣ 4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing"));
eligibility and budgets remain fixed within each task. Main tables
report mean and sample standard deviation (SD) across three runs.

details aggregation and uncertainty.

### 5.2 Baselines

Base model makes one attempt (Pass@1); best-of-$`N`$ (BoN) selects from
six candidates using VbD’s initial Evaluator. On AutomationBench,
self-preference (SP) follows VbD’s schedule with both harnesses fixed.

Among adaptive methods, Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) searches Actor
policies ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib28)), Retrospective Harness
Optimization (RHO) diagnoses earlier executions ([Pan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18)), and Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI) uses
preference history ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)). Red Queen Gödel
Machine (RQGM) co-evolves agents and evaluators ([Iacob et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)); our adaptation preserves staged search and
best-belief replacement. Evaluation is fixed within each stage;
replacement renews dependent statistics.

All methods include instructions, skills, and working rubrics; evolving
baselines reset per task. Permitted task observations replace HGM’s
benchmark utility and RQGM’s labeled anchors
(Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Baseline Adaptations ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")).
Configurations appear in
Tables [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Shared settings and model configurations. ‣ B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
and [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3 Baseline Adaptations ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results"),
and inference costs in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.3 RQ1: Task Performance at Test Time ‣ 5 Experiments").
The unranked external feedback reference ($`\dagger`$) runs HGM search
under fixed benchmark scoring.

### 5.3 RQ1: Task Performance at Test Time

*Does co-evolving execution and verification improve task performance?*
VbD achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods
without external feedback on all three task sets
(Tables [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments")–[3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 RQ1: Task Performance at Test Time ‣ 5 Experiments")).
The gains span workflow execution, interactions requiring policy
compliance, and professional deliverables, supporting the value of
improving execution and verification together.

The gains extend to professional deliverables: VbD leads all nine GDPval
sectors, with 82.4% overall rubric quality versus RQGM’s 80.1%. On
AutomationBench, selected outputs also satisfy more individual
requirements, as shown by higher partial credit
(Appendix [B.7](#A2.SS7 "B.7 Partial Task Completion ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")).

The evidence differs across tasks, but verification serves a common
purpose: inspection findings connect the Actor’s actions to observable
task requirements. This grounds adaptation in evidence about completion
while keeping the task requirements fixed, allowing the same findings to
guide both execution and verification.

### 5.4 RQ2: Internal Signal for Co-evolution

*How does the internal signal support selection and Actor updates?* We
assess Actor update decisions within each method’s own evolution runs
and Evaluator selection on a shared, fixed BoN candidate pool.

We label an Actor proposal as an improvement or regression by comparing
its output’s offline partial credit with the output it was evaluated
against, using valid, non-tied pairs. TP and FP count accepted
improvements and regressions; TN counts rejected regressions. We report

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{TNR}=\frac{\mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP}},\qquad\mathrm{Precision}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}}.
``` |  |

![Refer to caption](2611.15276v1/vbd_quality_control.png)

Figure 4: AutomationBench. (a) Actor update gating within each method’s
own evolution runs: TNR and precision. (b) Evaluator selection from
shared, fixed BoN pools: pass rate and partial credit.

VbD rejects 89.3% of observed regressions compared with 71.2% for RQGM,
while maintaining similar precision (77.6% versus 77.0%;
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.4 RQ2: Internal Signal for Co-evolution ‣ 5 Experiments")(a)).
This advantage of 18.1 percentage points in regression rejection
accompanies an update acceptance rate similar to those of HGM and RQGM
(Appendix [B.9](#A2.SS9.SSS0.Px2 "Update gating. ‣ B.9 Statistical Reporting ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")).

Incomplete verification can overlook successful outputs already in the
candidate pool. To isolate selection, we compare VbD’s and RQGM’s final
Evaluators with BoN’s initial Evaluator on six fixed BoN outputs per
task
(Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.4 RQ2: Internal Signal for Co-evolution ‣ 5 Experiments")(b);
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Evaluator Selection Quality ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")).
VbD exceeds both BoN and RQGM, improving pass rate by 4.6 percentage
points and partial credit by 2.4 over BoN. Since the available outputs
are unchanged, these gains come from selecting better work already in
the pool. Marketing088 illustrates the change in feedback: consistently
applying the response-scope requirement gives the selector a basis to
distinguish similar recorded actions and select an existing passing
output
(Appendix [C.7](#A3.SS7 "C.7 Evolved Verification for Selection ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.5 RQ3: Active Verification and Evaluator Evolution

*What do acquiring evidence and adapting verification each contribute?*
The variant *without active verification* assesses existing traces
without new inspections while retaining harness evolution. The variant
*without Evaluator evolution* inspects candidates with fixed Evaluator
instructions, rubrics, and skills while the Actor evolves. Tasks,
initial harnesses, base model, three-round schedule, and strict Actor
acceptance rule are shared.

Both removals lower the mean score on every task set while Actor
evolution remains active
(Tables [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments")–[3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 RQ1: Task Performance at Test Time ‣ 5 Experiments")).
On AutomationBench, removing active verification lowers the mean by 2.7
percentage points, and freezing the Evaluator lowers it by 1.6. Banking
and GDPval follow the same pattern.

The ablations distinguish acquiring evidence from retaining verification
lessons. A frozen Evaluator still gathers observations, but its
instructions, rubrics, and skills remain unchanged. Its lower scores
support carrying lessons forward: missed requirements motivate
persistent checks, and successful inspections supply reusable
procedures. Active verification expands the evidence for current
judgments, while Evaluator evolution adapts future checks under fixed
task requirements. Actor evolution cannot fully compensate.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.6 RQ4: Co-evolution in Practice

*How does a verification finding improve both execution and feedback?*
The cases trace how findings become reusable actions and checks through
two paths: exposing a missed requirement and discovering an operation
the Actor can reuse.

In Sales063, initial attempts omit customer-record updates and violate a
reply restriction
(Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ C.3 Press Release Distribution ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution")).
Verification accepts an untested claim that the service is unavailable
and overlooks the restriction. VbD adds an Actor skill for reply scope
and a matching Evaluator criterion; the next attempt completes the
updates and satisfies the restriction. HGM and RQGM complete the main
actions but retain replies naming excluded attendees. The case shows how
a missed requirement becomes guidance for both execution and assessment.

In Marketing015, the Evaluator retrieves a contact sheet through an
operation the Actors missed. The successful retrieval becomes an Actor
instruction and an Evaluator availability check
(Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction")); distribution then
succeeds. The initial Evaluator also recognizes success. Verification
supplies more than a verdict here: it reveals an action the Actor can
reuse and a check for future claims that a resource is unavailable.

Other cases show why output selection and Actor adoption are separate
decisions. Support091 recovers an earlier passing output despite failed
fresh attempts. Sales047 selects a passing new output but withholds the
Actor update because the final comparison lacks strict support
(Appendix [C.8](#A3.SS8 "C.8 Success without Actor Adoption ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution")).
Verification can still misinterpret evidence: Finance024 treats a file
timestamp as a business date and selects a failing output
(Appendix [C.9](#A3.SS9 "C.9 Failure in Date Interpretation ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution")).

Actor behavior complements these cases: attempts containing state
verification rise from 20.4% in Round 1 to 25.3% in Round 3
(Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Skill Use and Verification Behavior ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")).
The cases trace how findings become Actor checks; the aggregate trend is
consistent with this transfer from verification to execution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 6 Conclusion

VbD co-evolves Actor and Evaluator harnesses through active
verification, comparative review, and separate retention. Across three
task sets and two backbones, it achieves the highest overall scores
among the compared methods without external feedback. Ablations and
fixed-candidate selection support improving execution alongside the
verification procedure that supplies the internal signal.

Together, these findings explain the value of evolving verification
alongside task execution. Active verification supplies evidence,
co-evolution turns findings into execution guidance and reusable checks,
and separate retention distinguishes successful outputs from supported
updates. Task requirements and model weights stay fixed; adaptation
changes how the agent executes, checks completion, and carries
verification findings into subsequent attempts. More broadly, VbD
suggests that test-time agent improvement can progress beyond choosing
among existing behaviors by evolving the procedures that produce and
evaluate feedback.

## Limitations

VbD relies on observable evidence and model-based judgments. The Actor,
Evaluator, and reviewer may share errors in interpreting evidence, so
active verification and comparative review cannot eliminate incorrect
selections or updates ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib26)).

Repeated trials require states or artifacts that can be isolated and
inspected. As with replay-based adaptation ([Pan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18)), irreversible actions and environments that cannot be
reset limit direct application. Delayed effects or inaccessible state
may also escape verification.

Our experiments evaluate three-round adaptation within individual tasks.
Transfer across tasks and sustained improvement over longer evolution
remain untested. Additional execution, verification, and harness
revision incur inference and tool-use costs; deployment latency also
depends on environment response times.

## Ethical Considerations

VbD studies tool-using agents on benchmark tasks. Errors in execution or
verification can lead to unintended messages, incorrect record updates,
or misleading deliverables. Harness adaptation retains fixed task
requirements and tool permissions. Deployment in real environments
should enforce these permissions, protect sensitive information in
execution logs and artifacts, and require human oversight for
consequential actions. Access to personal or business data should be
limited to the authorized task, and use or redistribution of benchmark
materials and derived artifacts should respect the applicable licenses
and access conditions.

VbD uses verification findings to guide both harnesses, while retaining
outputs and updates through separate decisions.

specifies how these decisions fit into one co-evolution round after
initialization.

$`\mathcal{D}`$. A tilde denotes a proposal; a superscript $`+`$ denotes
the retained state after the round. Actor state includes persistent
check plans. Without an Evaluator proposal, $`\Phi^{+}=\Phi`$; without
an Actor proposal, both fresh attempts use $`H`$.

$`\widetilde{H},\widetilde{\Phi}`$; incumbent $`z`$, candidate set
$`\mathcal{G}`$, history $`\mathcal{D}`$

them to $`\mathcal{G}`$

3 $`F\leftarrow\mathcal{F}_{\Phi}(\mathcal{B})`$

selected candidate satisfy both strict comparisons; otherwise set
$`H^{+}\leftarrow H`$
(Equation [5](#S4.E5 "In Actor retention. ‣ 4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing"))

### A.1 Evidence, Selection, and Updates

Both Evaluators inspect a common candidate pool with their respective
harnesses fixed during each inquiry. Findings identify the candidate,
proposition, observations, and assessment
(Equation [1](#S4.E1 "In 4.2 Agentic Evaluation ‣ 4 Verify by Doing")).
The selector interprets these findings against the task requirements,
including observed defects and unresolved requirements. A supported
finding may establish a defect, such as excessive page count; its
consequence for the task determines the preference, rather than the
number of supported findings.

Evaluator adoption requires a valid trial and agreement in both review
orders. The retained Evaluator supports output selection; Actor adoption
additionally requires strict support for the proposed Actor’s own output
(Equation [5](#S4.E5 "In Actor retention. ‣ 4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing")).
Fallback selections leave the Actor unchanged.

The editor uses findings and trial history, including rejected
proposals, to update either or both harnesses. Each proposal connects an
observed gap to an expected change in execution or verification. Task
requirements, tool permissions, model weights, controller instructions,
and acceptance rules remain fixed. VbD returns the final selected
output, then resets its harnesses and history.

## Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results

Unless otherwise stated, empirical analyses use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
under the settings in
Tables [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Shared settings and model configurations. ‣ B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")–[5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Shared settings and model configurations. ‣ B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results").
We use offline benchmark scores to assess the complete loop, selection
by the evolved Evaluator, and Actor retention. Ablations test evidence
acquisition and persistent verification updates. Only the external
feedback reference uses these scores during evolution
(Appendix [B.8](#A2.SS8 "B.8 Evolution with External Feedback ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")).

### B.1 Execution Schedule

All iterative methods use three rounds with two Actor executions per
round, totaling six attempts per task per run. For VbD, Round 1 runs the
initial Actor twice to initialize the candidate pool and select an
incumbent; no harness update is adopted in this round. Rounds 2–3 test
current and proposed Actors using proposals prepared in the preceding
round. SP uses the same schedule and budgets with fixed harnesses.

To keep execution and assessment aligned, each candidate records its
generating harness and resulting state or deliverable. Evaluators
inspect a common pool, and selection uses the retained Evaluator’s
findings, with further inspection as needed. An earlier candidate
remains available through its saved output and state.

#### Comparison stages and candidate sets.

Evaluator qualification uses the common review pool $`\mathcal{B}`$;
output selection uses the eligible pool
$`\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{G}`$, which may include earlier attempts.
Candidate eligibility is fixed throughout evolution and excludes offline
task-success labels. Reused evidence retains its candidate identity and
observation scope. The main experiments and ablations apply the
retention rules in
Equations [3](#S4.E3 "In Evaluator adoption. ‣ 4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing")
and [5](#S4.E5 "In Actor retention. ‣ 4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing"),
with the comparison procedure described in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Complete Evolution Procedure").

After the retention decisions, the editor proposes changes to
instructions, rubrics, skills, or persistent check plans and specifies
how to test them. Both fresh Actors receive the same temporary checks;
only the proposed Actor receives persistent edits. Temporary checks
expire after the round unless reconsidered. History records component
sources, executed checks, and retention decisions. Changes to persistent
Actor check plans count as Actor proposals even when the other harness
text is unchanged.

#### Budget boundaries.

Operations are bounded by their assigned response limits and remaining
task allowance. When no response remains, execution terminates with an
error and produces no completed prediction.

### B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration

The AutomationBench public set (v1.0.5) contains 600 tasks, with 100 in
each of six workflow domains. Banking contains 97 tasks, with success
requiring both the correct final database state and the required
communication actions. These task sets evaluate completed interactions;
GDPval extends the comparison to professional deliverables.

GDPval selection covers tasks supported by our text and document tools:
spreadsheet contents, document structure, measurable formatting, and
editable chart data. We select 133 of the 220 public gold tasks,
covering nine sectors and 41 occupations.

Selection follows task requirements and reference availability, without
filtering by method scores. All methods use the same task IDs and
complete rubrics.

For evaluation, AutomationBench and $`\tau^{3}`$ Banking score each
method’s final selected output. Pass rate uses the full task
denominator; unresolved grades receive no pass credit. Base model makes
one attempt, while the other methods submit their selected candidate.
All task-local harnesses reset between tasks.

The single-attempt control uses the first BoN candidate, including
failed attempts. GPT-5.6-sol with xhigh reasoning effort grades
deliverables using official rubrics and expert artifacts. Task scores
apply criterion weights and retain penalties; sector scores average
their tasks, and overall scores average all 133 tasks within each run.
We report the mean and sample SD across three runs. These are local
rubric scores, distinct from official expert pairwise win rates. Rubrics
and expert artifacts are used for offline scope review and scoring,
except in the external feedback reference.

#### Shared settings and model configurations.

Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Shared settings and model configurations. ‣ B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
lists the shared execution limits and evolution protocol;

gives parameter counts and model-specific inference settings for
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Full role specifications
appear in Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Harness Specification").

### B.3 Baseline Adaptations

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Method |  Updated components |  Adaptation / selection procedure |
|  Base model |  No updates |  One Actor attempt. |
|  BoN ($`N=6`$) |  No updates |  Select among six candidates from one round. |
|  Self-preference |  No updates |  Agentic Evaluation and output retention under VbD’s schedule. |
|  HGM |  Actor |  Posterior-guided Actor policy search with a fixed Evaluator. |
|  RHO |  Actor |  Diagnose prior executions of the current task; guide updates by self-preference with a fixed Evaluator. |
|  RHI |  Actor instructions |  Revise instructions from task-local harness and pairwise preference history with a fixed Evaluator. |
|  RQGM (adapted) |  Actor and Evaluator |  Staged co-evolution with best-belief Evaluator replacement using permitted task feedback. |
|  VbD |  Actor and Evaluator |  Coupled Actor–Evaluator adaptation with comparative verification and separate update acceptance and output selection. |

Table 6: Harness configurations used in our comparisons. All methods
include instructions, skills, and working rubrics. Updates and candidate
comparisons vary by method; evolving harnesses reset for each task.

Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3 Baseline Adaptations ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
summarizes the evaluated configurations;
Table [7](#A2.T7 "Table 7 ‣ RQGM utility estimation. ‣ B.3 Baseline Adaptations ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
compares the original formulations. HGM uses a utility posterior for
Actor search and final selection \[[Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib28)\].
Our budget of six attempts limits runtime and token costs, but may
reduce HGM and RQGM’s tree search to an effectively linear sequence of
updates.

RHO originally improves a harness for future tasks by diagnosing grouped
rollouts on a coreset of past tasks. It proposes harness changes from
these diagnoses and accepts the best proposal only when its mean
pairwise self-preference is strictly positive \[[Pan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18)\]. Our adaptation retains retrospective diagnosis and
self-preference-guided Actor updates within the current task. Earlier
executions of that task supply the diagnostic history in place of a
cross-task coreset, and subsequent attempts test the revised Actor
within the six-execution budget. The Evaluator remains fixed throughout
adaptation.

RHI originally revises a textual harness using accumulated pairwise
preferences between successive executions, with a fixed Evaluator; its
stopping criterion aggregates improvement across tasks \[[Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)\]. Our adaptation retains task-specific instruction
revision from harness and preference history. Each round executes two
candidates within the shared six-execution budget, using task-local
feedback and a fixed Evaluator.
Table [11](#A2.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Update gating. ‣ B.9 Statistical Reporting ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
reports the RHI acceptance statistics.

Both adaptations use the execution and response limits in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Shared settings and model configurations. ‣ B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results").
Harnesses and histories reset between tasks, and benchmark scores remain
reserved for offline evaluation.

RQGM additionally changes the Evaluator between search stages. In the
original method, evaluation remains fixed within each search stage;
replacement uses the highest best-belief score on labeled anchors,
optionally augmented with an adversarial objective, and ties retain the
incumbent \[[Iacob et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)\]. Our task-local
adaptation preserves this structure and replacement rule but estimates
utility from permitted task observations. Report comparisons supply
evidence for that estimate. Replacement excludes statistics dependent on
the displaced Evaluator from subsequent search, while earlier outputs
remain available for reassessment.

VbD instead reviews Evaluator proposals within each co-evolution trial
and applies the separate retention rules in
Equations [3](#S4.E3 "In Evaluator adoption. ‣ 4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing")
and [5](#S4.E5 "In Actor retention. ‣ 4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing").

#### RQGM utility estimation.

For each Evaluator–candidate pair, the fixed assessment procedure
records whether the report’s material findings follow from observed
evidence and applicable task requirements. Supported assessments
contribute to $`S`$; evidenced incorrect claims, inapplicable criteria,
or material omissions contribute to $`F`$. Insufficient evidence
contributes to neither count. Each pair contributes at most one
observation; reassessment updates that observation. A report correctly
identifying a failed Actor attempt can therefore receive positive
utility. We compute the replacement score as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{BB}_{\epsilon}(e)=Q_{\epsilon}\!\left[\operatorname{Beta}(1+S_{e},1+F_{e})\right].
``` |  | (7) |

Here $`Q_{\epsilon}`$ denotes the $`\epsilon`$-quantile, with
$`\epsilon=0.05`$ by default. At a stage boundary, the highest-scoring
observed Evaluator replaces the incumbent only on a strict improvement;
ties retain the incumbent, and an unobserved alternative cannot displace
it.

| Method | Adapted components | Feedback | Scope |
|----|----|----|----|
| Actor harness optimization |  |  |  |
| GEPA \[[Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)\] | Prompts and instructions | Validation metric + reflection | Across a task set |
| HGM \[[Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib28)\] | Agent code | Benchmark utility | Descendant search |
| RHO \[[Pan et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)\] | Tools, skills, instructions | Diagnosis + self-preference | Future tasks (offline) |
| RHI \[[Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)\] | Agent loop instructions | Pairwise preference history | Within a task |
| TTHE \[[Nie et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)\] | Executable harness | Traces + proxy signals | Across batches |
| Actor–Evaluator co-evolution |  |  |  |
| RQGM \[[Iacob et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)\] | Actor + Evaluator programs | Utility + held-out labels | Across search stages |
| VbD (ours) | Actor + Evaluator harnesses | Executed checks; no labels | Within a task; reset |
| Adversarial evaluation |  |  |  |
| AIChilles \[[Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)\] | Candidate test workloads | Differential execution | Program regressions |

Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3 Baseline Adaptations ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results").

### B.4 Evaluator Selection Quality

To isolate selection quality, we hold Actor outputs fixed. We compare
BoN’s initial Evaluator with RQGM’s and VbD’s final retained Evaluators
on the same six BoN candidates per task. Each Evaluator uses its own
inspection procedure to select one output on each of the 600
AutomationBench tasks. VbD uses the Evaluator retained by
Equation [3](#S4.E3 "In Evaluator adoption. ‣ 4.3 Comparative Selection ‣ 4 Verify by Doing"),
keeping the initial version if no update is adopted. All selectors use
both presentation orders; disagreement is resolved by selecting the
smallest original candidate identifier. We report pass rate and partial
credit averaged across three runs.

Pass rate is 35.8% for VbD’s Evaluator, 33.4% for RQGM’s Evaluator, and
31.2% for the BoN baseline
(Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.4 RQ2: Internal Signal for Co-evolution ‣ 5 Experiments")(b)).
Partial credit is 69.8%, 68.5%, and 67.4%, respectively. VbD’s evolved
Evaluator exceeds BoN by 4.6 percentage points in pass rate and 2.4 in
partial credit.

### B.5 Evaluation Across Model Backbones

With Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, VbD reaches 48.4% on AutomationBench, 57.4% on
Banking, and 84.7% rubric quality on GDPval, leading the compared
methods without external feedback in all three overall scores
(Tables [8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ B.5 Evaluation Across Model Backbones ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")–[10](#A2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ B.5 Evaluation Across Model Backbones ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")).
On AutomationBench, it exceeds RQGM by 3.3 percentage points overall and
achieves the highest mean score in all six domains among methods without
external feedback. It also leads in all nine GDPval sectors. The gains
hold across both backbones.

The Qwen3.8-Flash-Next evaluation uses the shared protocol and model
settings in
Tables [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Shared settings and model configurations. ‣ B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")–[5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Shared settings and model configurations. ‣ B.2 Tasks, Scoring, and Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results").
Baseline schedules follow
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Baselines ‣ 5 Experiments"). Offline scoring
uses the same task sets and three-run aggregation as the
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 evaluation.

### B.6 Evolution Trajectories and Inference Cost

Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.3 RQ1: Task Performance at Test Time ‣ 5 Experiments")
pairs each round’s selected-output pass rate with cumulative tokens per
task. Cost includes Actor execution, harness editing, evaluation,
comparative review, and output selection; it excludes offline grading
and the fixed-candidate Evaluator analysis. Each method is plotted at
its incurred cost, with final pass rates and SDs from
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments"). All compared methods
generate six Actor candidates per task (BoN-6: six one-shot samples;
VbD: two per round over three rounds).

VbD gains 4.3 percentage points from Round 1 to Round 2 and a further
2.7 in Round 3, reaching 37.0%. Its second-round mean of 34.3% already
exceeds RQGM’s final 33.7% at a lower plotted cumulative cost.

### B.7 Partial Task Completion

Pass rate credits a task only when all scored checks pass.
AutomationBench also provides partial credit, the fraction of scored
assertions satisfied for each task \[[Shepard and Salimans,
2026](#bib.bib21)\]. Averaging these fractions reveals progress that
binary task completion can conceal.

Figure 6: Partial credit on AutomationBench. Scores average the fraction
of satisfied assertions per task with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. BoN is
shown as a horizontal baseline. Shading shows $`\pm`$ SD.

Figure [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ B.7 Partial Task Completion ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
shows VbD increasing from 66.35% to 70.26%, a gain of 3.91 percentage
points. RHO increases from 62.83% to 66.83%. VbD exceeds BoN from
Round 2 onward and finishes 1.63 percentage points above the strongest
baseline, RQGM. This complements the results on pass rate: later outputs
satisfy a larger fraction of scored requirements.

### B.8 Evolution with External Feedback

The external feedback reference uses HGM to evolve the Actor under fixed
model weights, with benchmark scores guiding updates and output
selection. AutomationBench and $`\tau^{3}`$ Banking supply outcome
checks; GDPval supplies local rubric scores. VbD and other baselines use
these scores only offline.

Tables [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Experiments")–[3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 RQ1: Task Performance at Test Time ‣ 5 Experiments")
compare the same task sets. The reference generates its own candidates,
whereas an oracle-selection bound requires a shared candidate
pool \[[Brown et al., 2024](#bib.bib3)\].

### B.9 Statistical Reporting

#### Aggregation and uncertainty.

Main result tables report mean $`\pm`$ sample SD across three evaluation
runs. Overall scores are computed within each run before aggregation; SD
is in percentage points, and rounding is applied only for display. Mean
differences are reported in percentage points. Behavioral bootstrap
intervals summarize variation across tasks using the procedures in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Behavioral Measurement Protocol ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution").

For GDPval,
Tables [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 RQ1: Task Performance at Test Time ‣ 5 Experiments")
and [10](#A2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ B.5 Evaluation Across Model Backbones ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
use the same 133 tasks and sector weights. Within each run, Overall
averages task scores, equivalently weighting sector means by sector task
counts. Its mean and sample SD are computed across the three run-level
Overall scores using unrounded values; each reported entry is then
rounded to one decimal place.

#### Update gating.

We assess Actor update decisions over the three-round evolution schedule
for each method, using offline partial-credit scores for the recorded
proposal–comparison pairs
(Table [11](#A2.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Update gating. ‣ B.9 Statistical Reporting ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")).
A proposal is positive if its output scores higher than its recorded
comparison output, and negative if it scores lower. TP counts accepted
improvements, FP counts accepted regressions, and TN counts rejected
regressions, using valid, non-tied offline partial-credit pairs. The
gate makes its decisions from public evidence; offline scores label the
outcomes for this analysis.

For each method, acceptance rate is $`N_{a}/N_{p}`$, where $`N_{p}`$ and
$`N_{a}`$ count all proposed and accepted updates. TNR is
$`\mathrm{TN}/(\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP})`$, and precision is
$`\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})`$; both use valid, non-tied
score pairs. All three metrics are percentages.

These measures describe different aspects of retention. Acceptance rate
gives its frequency, TNR measures rejection of observed regressions, and
precision measures the fraction of improvements among accepted updates.
VbD’s higher TNR accompanies similar precision and acceptance rates to
RQGM. The observed distinction is therefore most pronounced in filtering
regressions. This analysis characterizes the complete retention
procedure, while the case histories show why an output can be selected
without accepting its producing Actor.

| Method | Proposed | Accepted |  TP   |  FP   |  TN   |
|--------|----------|----------|-------|-------|-------|
| HGM    | 1,200    | 227      |  158  |  56   |  108  |
| RHO    | 1,432    | 698      |  302  |  121  |  89   |
| RHI    | 1,723    | 1,412    |  198  |  240  |  97   |
| RQGM   | 1,200    | 231      |  164  |  49   |  121  |

## Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution

The following recorded cases use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and trace how
verification findings change execution instructions, evaluation
criteria, and output selection. They also document updates that are
rejected and findings that are misinterpreted, showing where additional
evidence does not lead to a better decision.

### C.1 Budget Verification

The budget task requires correct payer attribution, consistent totals,
and tax-adjusted net revenue
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction")). The initial Evaluator
checks labels and headers but leaves the numerical relationships
untested. A proposed skill inspects expense and revenue cells through
four table probes. Both review orders favor this procedure, while the
earlier workbook remains selected.

The figure’s nine sum checks and seven net checks are offline
recomputations from the returned cells that establish arithmetic
consistency for those cells. Payer attribution requires comparing the
workbook’s assignments with source records.

### C.2 Grant Spending

The grant task classifies spending relative to elapsed project time. An
updated skill uses Python to recompute elapsed time and apply the task’s
thresholds to the recorded spending percentage. For the sampled award,
about 16.5% of the period has elapsed while 99.6% of the funds are
spent, satisfying the rapid-spending condition. This check supports
retaining the workbook, although later checks in the episode fail to
execute
(Listing [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).

### C.3 Press Release Distribution

In Marketing015, both initial Actors fail to read the contact
spreadsheet and send no task emails. The Evaluator retrieves the rows
through an alternative operation, prompting an Actor retrieval
instruction and an Evaluator skill for checking resource availability.
In Round 2, the proposed Actor follows the instruction to send the
release to three eligible outlets and a summary to the team. Inspection
checks a sent release and the summary; both harness updates are adopted,
and the passing output remains selected in Round 3. The Actor follows
the revised instructions without explicitly loading a skill, and the
initial Evaluator also recognizes success. The update therefore supplies
a missing retrieval procedure and a check on claims of resource
unavailability
(Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).

![Refer to caption](2611.15276v1/vbd_case_hiring.png)

Figure 7: Sales063: execution and verification across rounds. Columns
trace HGM, RQGM, and VbD using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on the same
AutomationBench task across three rounds. The comparison highlights the
missed reply restriction.

### C.4 Webinar Follow-up

Sales063 requires personalized follow-up emails, updated customer
records, and a final reply describing only completed actions.
Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ C.3 Press Release Distribution ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution")
and
Table [12](#A3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ C.4 Webinar Follow-up ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution")
trace this task’s execution across three rounds.

In Round 1, both initial attempts send follow-up emails but omit updates
to customer records and discuss excluded attendees. The selected attempt
claims the record service is unavailable without testing it. The
Evaluator accepts that explanation and misses the reply restriction. The
editor proposes a skill for checking the Actor’s final reply and a
corresponding Evaluator rubric.

In Round 2, the proposed Actor loads the skill, updates the customer
record and attendance, and reports only completed actions. Inspection
finds the requested update in its saved state and no matching record in
the earlier attempt. The proposed Evaluator checks both the saved state
and reply scope, testing the earlier claim of service unavailability
against observable results \[[Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib26)\]. Both
updates are accepted, and the selected output passes offline scoring.

In Round 3, a further proposal tests service availability before
declaring a limitation. It is not adopted, and the successful Round 2
output remains selected.

HGM and RQGM complete the customer-record updates and emails but retain
replies that name excluded attendees. HGM checks the saved records and
emails in Round 2 yet retains the reply “Not contacted (below
threshold).” RQGM distinguishes the updated engagement threshold from a
superseded rule and tests an Evaluator update concerning a deleted test
lead. That trial produces no findings with stronger evidential support,
so RQGM retains its Evaluator and earlier output. VbD’s paired updates
instead incorporate the missed reply restriction into both execution
guidance and assessment.

### C.5 Supplier Strategy

The supplier task requests a two- to three-page strategy. An initial
six-page preview prompts Actor instructions to shorten and check the
draft and Evaluator instructions to inspect its rendered length. Both
fresh previews show three pages; VbD selects the proposed Actor’s draft
and adopts the proposed Evaluator.

HGM detects excessive length but retains a four-page draft. RQGM tests a
stricter page-limit policy, but both Evaluators already detect the fresh
drafts’ excess length. It therefore retains its Evaluator and earlier
selected draft.

A common-renderer audit finds four pages for HGM, three for RQGM, and
two for VbD
(Figure [8](#A3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ C.4 Webinar Follow-up ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution"));
both RQGM and VbD meet the requested range. RQGM also claims that two
domestic suppliers have been identified, whereas the supplied evidence
concerns domestic capability. HGM and VbD describe the search as
proposed work. VbD retains its draft and adopts another Evaluator
update; some content requirements remain unresolved.

### C.6 Evolving Verification of Earlier Attempts

In Support091, the Actor remains fixed while revised verification
recovers an earlier successful output. The task requires consolidating
duplicate tickets, sending notifications, and logging completed actions
without mentioning untouched items in the reply. Round 2 finds no
supported difference between the compared outputs and retains the
initial selection. In Round 3, inspection revisits the same earlier pair
and detects excluded-item narration in the initial output. An Evaluator
update is adopted, and the passing Round 2 candidate is selected even
though both fresh Round 3 attempts fail.

### C.7 Evolved Verification for Selection

Marketing088 tests whether revised verification can identify a
successful output when candidate availability is fixed
(Figure [9](#A3.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ C.6 Evolving Verification of Earlier Attempts ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution")).
All selectors receive the same six independently generated BoN outputs.
The retained Evaluator selects a passing candidate in both presentation
orders, addressing the incomplete-feedback problem described in
Section [1](#S1 "1 Introduction").

The task requires invoicing overdue approved sponsors, applying
Finance’s processing requirements, and updating the tracker; the final
summary must list only acted-on items. Candidates A and B each record
three invoice sends totaling \$7,200, status updates, and a
reconciliation email. A also lists five skipped sponsors and their
exclusion reasons, whereas B reports completed actions without
enumerating exclusions.

In the reversed presentation, the initial Evaluator finds no material
difference among the most complete candidates on their recorded business
effects. The retained Evaluator checks reply scope against the original
instruction and distinguishes A from B in both orders. Its
reversed-order inquiry also confirms B’s three updated tracker statuses.
The reply check thus supplies a relevant distinction that the comparison
of business effects alone misses.

Self-preference and the initial Evaluator each choose B in the forward
order and A in the reversed order; the shared fallback rule resolves the
disagreement to A. The retained Evaluator chooses B in both orders.
Independent offline checks mark A as failing with 84.2% partial credit
and B as passing with 100%. These labels are unavailable during
selection.

Figure 10: Sales047: a passing output selected without Actor adoption.
For DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on AutomationBench, the final comparison
lacks strict support for retention. Bottom-row outcomes come from
offline checks unavailable during selection.

### C.8 Success without Actor Adoption

In the customer-health scoring task Sales047, a successful output is
selected without adopting its Actor update
(Figure [10](#A3.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ C.7 Evolved Verification for Selection ‣ Appendix C Case Studies of Harness Co-evolution")).
In Round 2, both nomination orders strictly favor the proposal for
retrieving the scoring policy and verifying persisted updates. Both
final comparisons declare equivalence: the reports acknowledge scores of
50 versus 35 but treat the difference as immaterial because both fall in
the same health category. The proposal is selected, but the absence of
strict final support blocks Actor adoption. Offline checks mark the
proposal as passing and both the incumbent and fresh parent attempt as
failing. The same passing output remains selected in Round 3.

### C.9 Failure in Date Interpretation

In Finance024, the selected invoice report passes after Rounds 1–2 but
fails after Round 3. The Evaluator substitutes the file’s write
timestamp for the report’s business date, assigns all six invoices to
the oldest overdue category, and selects a failing output over the
passing incumbent. No harness update is adopted. The failure results
from interpreting the observed timestamp as evidence of a different
event.

Marketing015 and Sales063 trace findings into changes to both roles,
whereas the budget case, Support091, and Marketing088 improve
verification or selection of existing work. Sales047 shows that
selecting a passing output need not lead to Actor adoption. The supplier
and date cases limit what can be concluded from individual checks: a
page count establishes length but not content coverage, and a file
timestamp does not by itself establish the report’s business date.

analyze DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731;

use Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Skill loading records explicit use of evolved
guidance, while Verify calls capture checks of action effects. These
measurements connect the case studies to aggregate changes in Actor
behavior.

|  Metric                       |  Round 1  |  Round 2  |  Round 3  |
|-------------------------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
|  Tool calls per attempt       |  63.8     |  51.8     |  54.6     |
|  Attempts with Verify (%)     |  20.4     |  24.0     |  25.3     |
|  Attempts loading skills (%)  |  0.0      |  22.2     |  23.1     |

Table 14: AutomationBench Actor behavior. The table reports calls per
attempt and rates of verification and skill loading for
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, following
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Behavioral Measurement Protocol ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution").

### D.1 Skill Use and Verification Behavior

For findings to improve execution, later Actors must use the guidance
produced by harness evolution. The share of attempts loading skills
rises from 0.0% in Round 1 to 23.1% in Round 3
(Table [14](#A4.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")).
This use of explicit guidance complements the cases in which a
discovered operation or missed requirement becomes a reusable Actor
skill.

![Refer to caption](2611.15276v1/vbd_behavior_shift.png)

Figure 11: Selected outcomes and Actor behavior in Rounds 1–3. For
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on AutomationBench, the top row estimates passing
selected outputs by tool-call count, normalized to round totals. The
middle row shows actions per attempt in five-call bins; the bottom row
magnifies Verify frequency. Dark gray curves show the Round 1 reference.
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Behavioral Measurement Protocol ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")
defines the measurements.

Figure 12: Behavioral changes by domain. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on
AutomationBench, panels show changes from Round 1 to Round 3 in Search
calls per attempt (left) and attempts with verification (right, pp).
Whiskers show 95% bootstrap intervals over tasks.

Later rounds use fewer Search calls and more Verify calls. Attempts
containing state verification rise from 20.4% to 25.3% between Rounds 1
and 3, while total calls per attempt fall from 63.8 to 54.6
(Table [14](#A4.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")).
Thus, more attempts include state checks even as the average execution
uses fewer calls. Search decreases in every domain, while verification
increases vary across domains
(Figure [12](#A4.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ D.1 Skill Use and Verification Behavior ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")).

The cross-method comparison with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next places VbD’s
increased checking in context
(Figure [13](#A4.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ D.1 Skill Use and Verification Behavior ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")).
HGM and RHI also reduce Search and Read, but their Verify frequency
remains flat or decreases.

RQGM shows a smaller change in Verify, while RHO remains relatively
stable across all three categories. VbD combines reduced Search with
increased Verify, a direction also seen in the external feedback
reference. This pattern is consistent with VbD’s design: verification
findings guide both output assessment and checks performed during
subsequent execution.
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Behavioral Measurement Protocol ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")
details the measurements.

These observations connect the Actor side of VbD to the Evaluator
results. On fixed candidates, the evolved Evaluator selects better
outputs
(Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Evaluator Selection Quality ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results"));
in later executions, Actors use evolved skills and check state more
often. The cases trace how shared findings link these changes, while the
ablations support both acquiring evidence and retaining improved checks
(Section [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 RQ3: Active Verification and Evaluator Evolution ‣ 5 Experiments")).
Together, these results support VbD’s central design: improve execution
and the verification procedure that supplies its internal signal within
the same task.

### D.2 Task Outcome Visualization

The task projection displays Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outcomes on individual
AutomationBench tasks.
Figure [14](#A4.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ D.2 Task Outcome Visualization ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")
projects TF-IDF task descriptions using 50-dimensional TruncatedSVD,
normalization, and t-SNE with PCA initialization and perplexity 35. Both
panels share 200 tasks and coordinates; outcome labels determine display
inclusion and annotations, while the projection uses task text. Orange
highlights VbD successes missed by all six candidates from the external
feedback reference. “Hard” and “Normal” are display labels for these
highlighted tasks and their context.

Figure 14: Task outcomes in t-SNE space. Using Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 200
AutomationBench tasks, panels compare (a) initialization with final

successes missed by the reference with external feedback in this

Green/red rings indicate label gains/losses across the same tasks.

### D.3 Behavioral Measurement Protocol

For each method and backbone, we analyze both Actor executions per round
on all 600 AutomationBench tasks across three runs, including failed
attempts and rejected proposals. We average counts and attempt-level
rates within tasks, then across tasks.

Table [15](#A4.T15 "Table 15 ‣ D.3 Behavioral Measurement Protocol ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution")
extends RHO’s action categories \[[Pan et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)\] with
explicit skill loading and other calls. Verify takes precedence over
Read and Search.

| Action  |  Recorded operation                               |
|---------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Search  |  Discover APIs or search for relevant records.    |
| Read    |  Retrieve a specified resource or state.          |
| Edit    |  Create, update, or delete records or artifacts.  |
| Execute |  Send, publish, submit, or transform data.        |
| Verify  |  Read the state after an earlier action.          |
| Skill   |  Explicitly load a skill.                         |
| Others  |  Tool names outside the standard taxonomy.        |

Table 15: Actor action categories. AutomationBench tool calls; Verify
marks state checks after actions.

Verify counts later read-backs of the same object after an action
without an explicit error; source consultation and prerequisite checks
remain Search or Read. All behavioral analyses use the same
object-matching rule. Verification and skill-loading rates count
attempts with at least one corresponding call.

#### Within-round trajectories.

In
Figure [11](#A4.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ D.1 Skill Use and Verification Behavior ‣ Appendix D Behavioral Dynamics of Evolution"),
step $`k`$ counts tool calls within an attempt. The top row estimates
the fraction of tasks with a passing selected output generated within
$`k`$ calls, normalized to each round’s pass rate. These curves follow
the selected output’s original execution, excluding discarded attempts
and controller work.

The middle row reports mean calls per attempt per position in five-call
bins; ended attempts contribute zero. The bottom row magnifies Verify on
the same basis. Count changes use relative percentages; share and
attempt-rate changes use percentage points.

Behavioral intervals resample tasks, retaining each task’s attempts and
rounds together. Initial-to-final changes use within-task differences,
and domain intervals resample within domains. Paired outcome comparisons
retain all 600 tasks, with unresolved grades receiving no pass credit.

## Appendix E Harness Specification

The harnesses express task requirements as procedures for execution and
verification. Role instructions define how each procedure operates;
recorded updates and executed checks show how an observed gap becomes
guidance that the agent can use.

### E.1 Role Policies and Verification

Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")
give the Actor instructions, and
Listing [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")
gives the Evaluator instructions. These accompany the task, working
rubric, available skills and tools, and assigned checks. Tool
availability follows the evaluated condition.

The Evaluator inspects unresolved requirements using the instructions
and tools in
Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification").
Returned observations guide further inquiry until completion or budget
exhaustion.

Skills check delivered effects and rule applicability, including
competing interpretations
(Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).
Both roles’ rubrics specify a criterion, a verification plan naming the
needed observations, a falsifier identifying contrary evidence, and an
unknown rule for unresolved evidence
(Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).

### E.2 Updates, Selection, and Recorded Use

The joint editor proposes changes and expected observations
(Listing [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).
Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")
specify Evaluator review and output preference;
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Execution Schedule ‣ Appendix B Experimental Setup and Results")
defines trials and retention.

In Marketing015, a successful lookup becomes an Actor retrieval
instruction and an Evaluator availability check
(Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).
Support091 instead pairs an adopted content criterion with message reads
that change selection between existing outputs
(Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).
Sales063 updates both roles around the reply restriction: an Actor skill
checks reply scope and an Evaluator rubric assesses the same requirement
(Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).
Listing [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")
records the rationale and expected observations for that proposal.

Two further records show why verification must remain tied to a
candidate’s own environment. Sales052 checks whether a policy was
available and reads the delivered message before judging its omission
(Listing [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).
Finance097 establishes that a newer status update was available to the
candidate and checks the delivered journal; the observation precedes the
skill adopted in the following round
(Listing [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).
The listings preserve the requests, returned evidence, and retention
decisions. Their Round 3 trials record no explicit skill loading; the
observations describe the full Evaluator procedure.

### E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks

For GDPval, the Actor creates and reopens deliverables; the Evaluator
inspects their contents and native structure
(Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).

Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")
specify the verification skills adopted for numerical requirements, with
an executed date-and-threshold check recorded in
Listing [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification").
The remaining examples reproduce executed programs for source coverage,
native workbook structure, and numerical consistency
(Listings [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")–[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Deliverables and Executable Checks ‣ Appendix E Harness Specification")).
Award reconciliation compares the complete qualifying ID set with the
delivered workbook. Pivot inspection tests for native workbook
components that displayed totals cannot establish. Capacity verification
recomputes a recurrence over the entered demand and capacity. Each
program is paired with its returned observation, so the reader can see
both the checked property and the inputs on which the conclusion
depends.
````
